Nomenclature

References

On this page

Arrays and clusters of spheres by the multipole expansion ​

The whole page as one script

Every block of this page, in order, is scripts/95_multipole_spheres.jl. From a clone of the repository, julia --project=docs -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()' once, then julia scripts/95_multipole_spheres.jl, runs it end to end.

Before this page

The multipole expansion method and its elastic counterpart, where the scheme is derived, and Particle assemblies and N-body schemes for the assemblies it acts on.

The multipole expansion method resolves the field around every sphere of an assembly, up to a degree nmax of the harmonics. This page computes with MultipoleExpansion the reference results of the method on spheres: the conductivity and the stiffness of the three cubic arrays tabulated by Kushch (2013) and Kushch and Sevostianov (2014), and the conductivity and the stiffness of the finite cluster of 27 spheres that serves as the test problem of the sample codes of Kushch (2013). The published values are read from the two files below.

julia
using MeanFieldHomogenization
using TensND
using LinearAlgebra
using JSON
using Markdown
using Printf
using Plots
gr()

# Interactive 3D helpers (Plotly through require.js).
include(joinpath(pkgdir(MeanFieldHomogenization), "scripts", "common", "docviz.jl"))

default(; left_margin = 5Plots.mm, bottom_margin = 5Plots.mm)

literature(key) = JSON.parsefile(joinpath(pkgdir(MeanFieldHomogenization), "data", "literature", key * ".json"))
book = literature("kushch2013")
paper = literature("kushch2014")
Data read above: data/literature/kushch2013.json 12 quantities, 102 records

Kushch, Volodymyr I. (2013). Micromechanics of Composites: Multipole Expansion Approach. Elsevier. ISBN 9780124076839. doi:10.1016/C2012-0-03565-X

Read in Tables 3.1 to 3.3 (p. 67), 5.1 to 5.3 (pp. 149-150), 6.3 and 6.4 (pp. 197-198), 7.6 (p. 244) and 7.7 to 7.10 (pp. 245-246); Appendix A, sections A.1 to A.4 and Table A.1 (p. 465) checked against the source

Transcribed from the published book (PDF), read on the page text

Conductivities are divided by that of the matrix, the contrast being the conductivity of the spheres over that of the matrix. The values of the appendix are the printouts the sample codes give as correct. Stiffnesses are divided by the shear modulus of the matrix as in the printed tables, the contrast being mu1/mu0.

Quantities

namevaluedescriptionwhere
fcm_conductivity1.53345Effective conductivity, over that of the matrix, of the finite cluster of 27 equal spheres on a 3x3x3 simple cubic block, volume fraction 0.2, contrast 10, closed by the modified Maxwell method (Eq. 2.65). Appendix A.1, p. 434
fcm_volume_fraction0.2Volume fraction of the spheres in the two finite-cluster test problems; the period of the block is (4 pi / (3 c))^(1/3) radii. Appendix A.1 and A.3
fcm_conductivity_contrast10.0Conductivity of the spheres over that of the matrix in the conduction test problem. Appendix A.1
periodic_conductivity_sc5.89112Effective conductivity, over that of the matrix, of the simple cubic array at the volume fraction 0.5 and the contrast 1e8 (Eq. 3.51). Appendix A.2, p. 439
fcm_bulk_modulus1.4064Effective bulk modulus over that of the matrix for the finite cluster of 27 spheres, volume fraction 0.2, shear moduli ratio 1e6, Poisson ratios 0.3 (Eq. 4.123). Appendix A.3, p. 446
fcm_shear_modulus_11.6568Effective shear modulus (C1111 - C1122)/2 over the shear modulus of the matrix, same problem (Eq. 4.124). Appendix A.3, p. 446
fcm_shear_modulus_21.4719Effective shear modulus C1212 over the shear modulus of the matrix, same problem (Eq. 4.125). Appendix A.3, p. 446
fcm_shear_contrast1.0e6Shear modulus of the spheres over that of the matrix in the elasticity test problem. Appendix A.3, p. 441
fcm_poisson_ratio0.3Poisson ratio of the matrix and of the spheres in the elasticity test problem. Appendix A.3, p. 441
ruc_c11331.12681C1133/(2 mu0) of the simple cubic array, as printed by the sample code of the periodic elasticity problem. Appendix A.4, p. 454
ruc_c33334.79979C3333/(2 mu0), same problem. Appendix A.4, p. 454
ruc_c12122.24677C1212/mu0, same problem. Appendix A.4, p. 454

Notes

  • The printed column header of the infinite contrast is the symbol of infinity.
  • Tables 3.1 to 3.3 are complete; Table A.1 goes to the degree 50 in the book, of which the degrees 2 to 8 are transcribed.
  • Table conductivity_sc: Table 3.1, p. 67. Effective conductivity of the simple cubic array of spheres, over that of the matrix.
  • Table conductivity_bcc: Table 3.2, p. 67. Effective conductivity of the body-centered cubic array of spheres, over that of the matrix.
  • Table conductivity_fcc: Table 3.3, p. 67. Effective conductivity of the face-centered cubic array of spheres, over that of the matrix.
  • Table lattice_sums_sc: Table A.1, p. 465. First rows of the lattice sums of the simple cubic lattice of unit period, divided by N_ts = sqrt((t-s)!(t+s)!): harmonic Y_ts(0) and biharmonic Z_ts(0). The harmonic sum of degree 2, conditionally convergent, is given in the convention of the book.
  • In the conductivity tables the columns contrast_0 to contrast_infinity are the conductivity of the spheres over that of the matrix; contrast_infinity stands for perfectly conducting spheres.
  • Table stiffness_sc: Table 5.1, p. 149. Effective stiffness of the simple cubic array of spheres, nu0 = nu1 = 0.3 (Section 5.7, p. 145): C1122/(2 mu0), C1111/(2 mu0) and C1212/mu0, the contrast being mu1/mu0.
  • Table stiffness_bcc: Table 5.2, p. 150. Effective stiffness of the body-centered cubic array of spheres, nu0 = nu1 = 0.3 (Section 5.7, p. 145): C1122/(2 mu0), C1111/(2 mu0) and C1212/mu0, the contrast being mu1/mu0.
  • Table stiffness_fcc: Table 5.3, p. 150. Effective stiffness of the face-centered cubic array of spheres, nu0 = nu1 = 0.3 (Section 5.7, p. 145): C1122/(2 mu0), C1111/(2 mu0) and C1212/mu0, the contrast being mu1/mu0.
  • Tables stiffness_bcc: the entries 2.6782 (c = 0.4, C1212, contrast 1000) and 6.2030 (c = 0.6, same column) are printed with four decimals in the book; they are transcribed as printed.
  • Table stiffness_spheroids: Table 7.6, p. 244, columns tmax = 15. C3333/mu0 of an orthogonal array of spheroids of semi-axes (1, 1, aspect_ratio), periods proportional to the semi-axes, nu0 = nu1 = 0.3, the contrast being mu1/mu0 (0 for cavities); the columns c_0.1 to c_0.5 are the volume fraction.
  • Table conductivity_cracks_so: Table 6.3, p. 197. Effective conductivity lambda*33/lambda0 of a solid with insulating penny-shaped cracks of unit radius and normal e3 on the orthogonal lattice of periods (a1, a1, a3), one crack per cell; the key a3_over_a1_1_2 is a3/a1 = 1/2, and a3_over_a1_0 the limit a3/a1 -> 0, which no computation at finite a3 reaches. The entry a1 = 4, a3/a1 = 1/2 is printed 0.932; the multipole expansion gives 0.923, the same digits transposed, in line with the body-centered array of the same crack density (0.919, Table 6.4): it is transcribed as printed.
  • Table conductivity_cracks_bc: Table 6.4, p. 198. The same with two cracks per cell, at the origin and at (a1/2, a1/2, a3/2) (body-centered array). The entries 0.0045 and 0.00005 are printed 0.45 · 10^-2 and 0.5 · 10^-4.
  • Tables young_cracks_so, shear_cracks_so, young_cracks_bc, shear_cracks_bc: Tables 7.7 to 7.10, pp. 245-246. E*33/E0 = 1/(E0 D*3333) and mu*13/mu0 = 1/(4 mu0 D*1313), D* the effective compliance, of a solid of Poisson ratio nu0 = 0.25 with traction-free penny-shaped cracks of unit radius and normal e3 on the lattice of periods (a, a, a3); the key a_over_a3_1_2 is a/a3 = 1/2. SO: one crack per cell; BC: two, at the origin and at (a/2, a/2, a3/2).

1. The simple cubic array ​

One sphere per cubic cell, of conductivity in a matrix of conductivity  . cubic_lattice builds the periodic assembly from the volume fraction, and the scheme returns the conductivity of the periodic medium, which is isotropic for a cubic array.

julia
matrix = Dict(:K => TensISO{3}(1.0))
spheres(k₁) = Dict(:K => TensISO{3}(k₁))
conductivity(asm, nmax) = canonical_components(homogenize(asm, MultipoleExpansion(; nmax), :K))[3, 3]

The table of Kushch and Sevostianov (2014) gives the conductivity to three decimals for five contrasts, the last being perfectly conducting spheres, represented here by  . Each cell below shows the value computed at nmax = 15 and, in parentheses, the published one.

julia
contrasts = (0.0, 10.0, 100.0, 1000.0, 1.0e8)
columns = ("contrast_0", "contrast_10", "contrast_100", "contrast_1000", "contrast_infinity")
headers = ("0", "10", "100", "1000", "∞")

function comparison(kind, rows; nmax = 15)
    io = IOBuffer()
    println(io, "| ``c`` | ", join(("``k_1/k_0 = $(h)``" for h in headers), " | "), " |")
    println(io, "| :-- | ", join(fill(":--", length(headers)), " | "), " |")
    for row in rows
        cells = map(zip(contrasts, columns)) do (k₁, column)
            k = conductivity(cubic_lattice(kind, matrix, spheres(k₁); fraction = row["c"]), nmax)
            @sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", k, row[column])
        end
        println(io, "| ", row["c"], " | ", join(cells, " | "), " |")
    end
    return Markdown.parse(String(take!(io)))
end

comparison(:sc, paper["tables"]["conductivity_sc"])

The two agree to the last digit up to the fraction 0.45. At the fraction 0.5 and a high contrast the degree 15 is not enough: the spheres almost touch (the fraction of contact is  ), and the field in the gap between two neighbors needs harmonics of high degree. The convergence is monotonic, and starts at nmax = 1 from the estimate of Maxwell and Mori–Tanaka, which the dipoles alone give exactly:

julia
degrees = 1:2:25
p_conv = plot(;
    xlabel = "nmax", ylabel = "k / k₀", legend = :right,
    title = "Simple cubic array, perfectly conducting spheres"
)
for c in (0.3, 0.4, 0.5)
    asm = cubic_lattice(:sc, matrix, spheres(1.0e8); fraction = c)
    plot!(p_conv, degrees, [conductivity(asm, n) for n in degrees]; marker = :circle, ms = 3, label = "c = $c")
    k_mt = canonical_components(homogenize(asm, MoriTanaka(), :K))[1, 1]
    scatter!(p_conv, [1], [k_mt]; marker = :star5, ms = 7, color = :black, label = c == 0.3 ? "Mori–Tanaka" : "")
end
published = last(paper["tables"]["conductivity_sc"])["contrast_infinity"]
hline!(p_conv, [published]; ls = :dash, color = :gray, label = "published, c = 0.5")
p_conv

The value printed by the sample code of Kushch (2013) for the fraction 0.5, with five decimals, is reached at nmax = 25, the degree that code uses:

julia
asm = cubic_lattice(:sc, matrix, spheres(1.0e8); fraction = 0.5)
(computed = conductivity(asm, 25), published = book["quantities"]["periodic_conductivity_sc"]["value"])
(computed = 5.891120737473517, published = 5.89112)

2. Body-centered and face-centered arrays ​

The cell of the body-centered array holds two spheres and that of the face-centered array four. Nothing changes in the call. At a given fraction the three arrays have the same estimate of Mori–Tanaka; the multipole expansion separates them, the more so as the spheres come close to contact, which happens at the fractions 0.524, 0.680 and 0.740.

julia
fractions(kind) = range(0.05, max_packing_fraction(kind) - 0.02; length = 15)
p_arrays = plot(;
    xlabel = "volume fraction c", ylabel = "k / k₀", legend = :topleft, yscale = :log10,
    title = "Cubic arrays, k₁/k₀ = 100"
)
for (kind, name, color) in ((:sc, "conductivity_sc", 1), (:bcc, "conductivity_bcc", 2), (:fcc, "conductivity_fcc", 3))
    cs = fractions(kind)
    ks = [conductivity(cubic_lattice(kind, matrix, spheres(100.0); fraction = c), 11) for c in cs]
    plot!(p_arrays, cs, ks; color, label = "$(kind), nmax = 11")
    rows = book["tables"][name]
    scatter!(p_arrays, getindex.(rows, "c"), getindex.(rows, "contrast_100"); color, marker = :diamond, label = "$(kind), published")
end
mt(c) = (1 + 2c * 99 / 102) / (1 - c * 99 / 102)
plot!(p_arrays, 0.05:0.01:0.7, mt; color = :black, ls = :dash, label = "Mori–Tanaka")
p_arrays

The curves pass through the published points, except at the last fraction of each array, where the degree 11 is short as in the simple cubic case.

3. A finite cluster of 27 spheres ​

The sample codes of Kushch (2013) take a block of    equal spheres on a simple cubic lattice, in the infinite matrix. The block is replaced by the homogeneous ball that holds the same fraction of spheres and sends the same far field, which is the closure of Maxwell; MixedBC carries that ball.

julia
function block(n, c, properties, matrix_properties)
    R = cbrt(3c / (4π))                        # radius of the spheres, for a unit period
    asm = ParticleAssembly(; boundary = MixedBC(R * cbrt(n^3 / c)))
    add_matrix!(asm, matrix_properties)
    for i in 1:n, j in 1:n, k in 1:n
        add_particle!(asm, Symbol(:p, i, j, k), (i, j, k) .- (n + 1) / 2, Ellipsoid(R), properties)
    end
    return asm
end

q(name) = book["quantities"][name]["value"]
cluster = block(3, q("fcm_volume_fraction"), spheres(q("fcm_conductivity_contrast")), matrix)

The spheres and the ball that closes the cluster:

julia
function cluster_scene(asm; uid)
    traces = String[]
    for name in particle_names(asm)
        R = particle_geometry(asm, name).semi_axes[1]
        X, Y, Z = ellipsoid_surface(R, R, R; center = particle_center(asm, name), nu = 17, nv = 9)
        push!(traces, surface_trace(X, Y, Z; color = "#4063D8"))
    end
    Rb = asm.boundary.shape.semi_axes[1]
    X, Y, Z = ellipsoid_surface(Rb, Rb, Rb; nu = 33, nv = 17)
    push!(traces, surface_trace(X, Y, Z; color = "#8c959f", opacity = 0.15))
    return plotly_scene(traces; uid, height = 480, title = "27 spheres at the fraction 0.2, in the ball of the same fraction")
end

cluster_scene(cluster; uid = "mem-cluster-27")

Stiffness ​

The elasticity problem has the same geometry, with nearly rigid spheres and the Poisson ratio 0.3 in both phases. The block has the cubic symmetry of its lattice, hence three moduli: the bulk modulus and the two shear moduli    and  , which a one-site estimate does not tell apart.

julia
iso(μ, ν) = TensISO{3}(2μ * (1 + ν) / (1 - 2ν), 2μ)        # (3k, 2μ)
ν = q("fcm_poisson_ratio")
C₀ = iso(1.0, ν)
k₀ = 2 * (1 + ν) / (3 * (1 - 2ν))
elastic = block(3, q("fcm_volume_fraction"), Dict(:C => iso(q("fcm_shear_contrast"), ν)), Dict(:C => C₀))

function moduli(scheme)
    M = mandel(homogenize(elastic, scheme, :C), CanonicalBasis{3, Float64}())
    return ((M[1, 1] + 2M[1, 2]) / 3k₀, (M[1, 1] - M[1, 2]) / 2, M[4, 4] / 2)
end

rows = [("Mori–Tanaka", moduli(MoriTanaka()))]
append!(rows, [("multipole expansion, nmax = $n", moduli(MultipoleExpansion(; nmax = n))) for n in (2, 4, 6)])
push!(rows, ("published", (q("fcm_bulk_modulus"), q("fcm_shear_modulus_1"), q("fcm_shear_modulus_2"))))
io = IOBuffer()
println(io, "| | ``k/k_0`` | ``\\mu_1/\\mu_0`` | ``\\mu_2/\\mu_0`` |\n| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |")
for (name, m) in rows
    @printf(io, "| %s | %.4f | %.4f | %.4f |\n", name, m...)
end
Markdown.parse(String(take!(io)))
$k/k_0$$\mu_1/\mu_0$$\mu_2/\mu_0$
Mori–Tanaka1.40381.52501.5250
multipole expansion, nmax = 21.40501.65031.4696
multipole expansion, nmax = 41.40641.65581.4717
multipole expansion, nmax = 61.40641.65681.4719
published1.40641.65681.4719

The bulk modulus hardly leaves the one-site estimate. The two shear moduli do, in opposite directions: the block resists a stretch along one of its axes with a contraction along another () more than a shear between two of its axes ().

4. Stiffness of the cubic arrays ​

On a periodic array, each sphere stands for its lattice in elasticity too (theory). Kushch (2013) tabulate the three moduli , and of the three cubic arrays for voids, spheres ten times stiffer than the matrix and nearly rigid ones, the Poisson ratio being 0.3 in both phases. Each cell gives the value computed at nmax = 8 and, in parentheses, the published one, for the fractions where this degree gives the third decimal.

julia
contrasts_el = (0, 10, 1000)
function stiffness_table(kind, name; cs = (0.1, 0.2, 0.3), nmax = 8)
    io = IOBuffer()
    println(io, "| ``c`` | ", join(("``\\mu_1/\\mu_0 = $(μ)``" for μ in contrasts_el), " | "), " |")
    println(io, "| :-- | ", join(fill(":--", length(contrasts_el)), " | "), " |")
    for row in book["tables"][name]
        row["c"] in cs || continue
        cells = map(contrasts_el) do μ₁
            asm = cubic_lattice(kind, Dict(:C => C₀), Dict(:C => iso(float(μ₁), ν)); fraction = row["c"])
            M = mandel(homogenize(asm, MultipoleExpansion(; nmax), :C), CanonicalBasis{3, Float64}())
            @sprintf(
                "%.3f, %.3f, %.3f (%.3f, %.3f, %.3f)", M[1, 2] / 2, M[1, 1] / 2, M[6, 6] / 2,
                row["c1122_contrast_$μ₁"], row["c1111_contrast_$μ₁"], row["c1212_contrast_$μ₁"]
            )
        end
        println(io, "| ", row["c"], " | ", join(cells, " | "), " |")
    end
    return Markdown.parse(String(take!(io)))
end

julia
let asm = cubic_lattice(:sc, Dict(:C => C₀), Dict(:C => iso(1000.0, ν)); fraction = 0.4)
    M = mandel(homogenize(asm, MultipoleExpansion(; nmax = 12), :C), CanonicalBasis{3, Float64}())
    computed = round.((M[1, 3] / 2, M[3, 3] / 2, M[6, 6] / 2); digits = 5)

5. Field around two spheres ​

The coefficients of the series give the field at any point of the matrix. Take two spheres ten times more conducting than the matrix, under a gradient along the line of their centers; multipole_coefficients returns the coefficients for the three unit gradients, and the temperature follows by summing the decaying harmonics of each sphere.

julia
centers = Dict(:upper => [0.0, 0.0, 0.55], :lower => [0.0, 0.0, -0.55])
pair = ParticleAssembly(; boundary = MixedBC(3.0))
add_matrix!(pair, matrix)
for (name, X) in centers
    add_particle!(pair, name, X, Ellipsoid(0.5), spheres(10.0))
end
nmax = 12
b = multipole_coefficients(pair; scheme = MultipoleExpansion(; nmax))

function temperature(x; gradient = 3)
    T = x[gradient]
    for (name, X) in centers
        Y = irregular_solid_harmonics(x - X, nmax)
        T += real(sum(b[name, n, m][gradient] * Y[n, m] for n in 1:nmax for m in (-n):n))
    end
    return T
end

The spheres are a tenth of a radius apart. Each one is nearly isothermal, and the temperature drop that the remote gradient would spread over the gap is concentrated in it: the map below is the temperature in a plane through the two centers, the matrix alone being colored.

julia
xs, zs = range(-1.3, 1.3; length = 131), range(-1.5, 1.5; length = 151)
inside(x, z) = any(X -> hypot(x, z - X[3]) < 0.5, values(centers))
field = [inside(x, z) ? NaN : temperature([x, 0.0, z]) for z in zs, x in xs]
p_field = heatmap(
    xs, zs, field; aspect_ratio = :equal, color = :balance, xlabel = "x₁", ylabel = "x₃", xlims = (-1.3, 1.3),
    colorbar_title = "T", title = "Temperature under a unit gradient along x₃"
)
